title: The Ledger of Small Things
text:
Creative nonfiction thrives on the tension between what happened and what it meant to the person who lived it. A writer reconstructing a childhood kitchen must choose which details to render with vividness and which to leave in shadow, knowing that every omission is itself a kind of testimony. The most durable memoirs therefore read less like inventories of events than like carefully calibrated arguments about memory.

Yet the genre's ethical obligations are rarely simple, particularly when the people portrayed cannot consent to their portrayal. Some authors respond by altering names and compressing timelines; others insist that such liberties dilute the testimony they set out to preserve. The debate, unresolved for decades, reveals how deeply memoir depends on trust between the one who remembers and the one who reads.

questions.text: According to the passage, what must a writer choose when reconstructing a childhood kitchen?
options: Which details to render vividly and which to leave in shadow
Whether to publish the memoir in a newspaper
Which relatives to invite to the house
How to avoid mentioning the kitchen at all

questions.text: According to the passage, what do some authors do in response to the ethical difficulties of portraying people who cannot consent?
options: They refuse to write about their families
They alter names and compress timelines
They publish their work only as fiction
They ask the subjects to write the book

questions.text: What does the passage imply about the most durable memoirs?
options: They are mainly lists of factual events
They depend on the reader's trust in the remembering voice
They avoid any discussion of ethics
They are written without any omissions

questions.text: The passage suggests that the debate over altering details is:
options: Resolved by a clear consensus among authors
Irrelevant to the question of trust
Unresolved and tied to the relationship between writer and reader

vocabulary.definition: the quality of being bright, clear, and detailed in description
a statement or evidence that shows that something is true
detailed lists of items or events
permission given by a person for something to happen

paragraph_translations: La no ficción creativa prospera en la tensión entre lo que sucedió y lo que significó para quien lo vivió. Un escritor que reconstruye la cocina de su infancia debe elegir qué detalles presentar con viveza y cuáles dejar en la sombra, sabiendo que cada omisión es también una forma de testimonio. Las memorias más duraderas se leen, por ello, menos como inventarios de hechos que como argumentos cuidadosamente calibrados sobre la memoria.

Sin embargo, las obligaciones éticas del género rara vez son sencillas, sobre todo cuando las personas retratadas no pueden dar su consentimiento a esa representación. Algunos autores responden alterando los nombres y comprimiendo las cronologías; otros insisten en que tales licencias diluyen el testimonio que pretendían preservar. El debate, sin resolver durante décadas, revela hasta qué punto la memoria depende de la confianza entre quien recuerda y quien lee.
